text:
B: Hello. Can you hear me?
A: Yes. Hello. I'm Helen.
B: Annelies. I'm in Sheffield.
A: Otley. So not too far, really.
B: No. Over the moors. Erm, I think I recognise your bookcase from the photograph.
A: It's hard to miss. I keep saying I'll sort it out.
B: You stack them sideways, I noticed. I do that too when the shelf is full. My husband says it looks like a library that's given up.
A: That's quite accurate. I work in an archive, so I've no excuse.
B: Oh, an archive. Which one?
A: Special collections, at a university in Leeds. Letters, diaries, mill records. I'm cataloguing a family's letters at the moment. Nineteenth century, mostly the women writing to each other. It's very slow work but I like it. You get to know their handwriting, and then you sort of get to know them.
B: That sounds lovely. I'm at the university here, but in the office side. Executive assistant to a head of faculty. Very little handwriting, a lot of committee papers.
A: Less romantic.
B: Much less. What are you reading at the moment, then? For yourself, I mean.
A: Erm, a Norwegian novel. I'm halfway through and I'm still not sure if I like it. Everybody stares at the sea a lot.
B: That's often the way with them. My book group is reading a Japanese one this month. There are five of us. Two loved it, two hated it, and I'm in the middle.
A: Which one?
B: About a woman who works in a convenience store. I can't remember the author, sorry.
A: Oh, I know it. I liked that one. I thought she was the only sensible person in it.
B: Yes, I thought that too, actually. I'll tell the group.
A: Do you walk? You've got the look of someone who walks. Sorry, that's an odd thing to say.
B: No, it's true. The Peak District, most weekends, with Graham. I take a small notebook and do watercolour sketches. Very bad ones.
A: I draw plants. Foxgloves, hedgerow things. Pencil, then a bit of watercolour.
B: Oh, the foxglove behind you. That's yours?
A: It is, yes.
B: It's not bad at all. It's very good.
A: Thank you. I don't show people usually.
B: No, I don't either. Graham has started baking sourdough. The whole kitchen is covered in flour.
A: I've had a starter going three years. It didn't rise at the weekend, though. I think it's sulking.
B: I'll tell him they sulk. He'll be relieved it's not him.
A: It's usually the weather. Or the flour. Never the baker.
B: That's what I'll say, then. Erm, I think we're nearly out of time.
A: Yes. It's been nice. Quiet, in a good way.
